payload.prompt: What does time on ice measure?

options.text: The number of minutes a player plays in a game.
How long a player can skate without stopping.
The total time a team plays in a period.

explanation.correct: Right. Time on ice (TOI) is how many minutes a player is actually on the ice during the game. The clock stops at whistles, so it's game time, not wall-clock time.
explanation.incorrect: TOI is simply the minutes a player plays. Top forwards and defensemen often play 18 to 25 minutes; fourth-liners may play closer to 8 to 10.
explanation.sayThisLine: His time on ice shows how much the coach trusts him.

payload.prompt: How many minutes does a star defenseman typically play per game?

explanation.correct: Right around 24 minutes. Star defensemen log heavy minutes because coaches lean on them at even strength and on special teams.
explanation.incorrect: Top-pair defensemen usually play around 22 to 26 minutes a night, because coaches use them in tough matchups and on both special teams.
explanation.sayThisLine: A 25-minute defenseman carries the load on his team.

payload.prompt: What is plus-minus?

options.text: Goals scored by the player minus shots he took.
Goals for while he is on the ice minus goals against at even strength.
A player's rating compared to his teammates.

explanation.correct: Yes. Plus-minus is a quick snapshot of the goals for and against while that player is on the ice at even strength (power-play goals don't count).
explanation.incorrect: Plus-minus counts goals for and goals against while the player is on the ice at even strength. If his team scores 3 and gives up 2 while he's playing, he's plus-1.
explanation.sayThisLine: Plus-minus is a rough guide, since it depends a lot on his linemates.

payload.prompt: Match the player stat to what it shows.

pairs.definition: The number of minutes a player plays in a game; shows usage and trust.
Goals for minus goals against while he is on the ice at even strength; a noisy snapshot.
The number of times a player goes on and off the ice; more shifts means more line changes.

explanation.summary: TOI tells you how much a coach uses a player. Plus-minus is a rough look at what happens while he's on the ice, and it is heavily shaped by his teammates.
explanation.sayThisLine: He plays big minutes, but his plus-minus is hurt by the team around him.

payload.prompt: Complete the statement about player minutes.
payload.template: A defenseman with {{toi}} of TOI is a {{role}} player, often facing {{matchups}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. About 24 minutes marks a top-pair defenseman, who often faces the other team's best forwards.
explanation.incorrect: Heavy minutes, around 22 to 26, are for a top-pair defenseman, who is usually sent out against the other team's best players.

payload.prompt: What does a team's Corsi of 55 percent mean?

options.text: The team is winning 55 percent of their games.
The team has 55 percent of the shot attempts in games.
55 percent of the team's shots go in.

explanation.correct: Right. Corsi (CF%) is the share of all shot attempts (shots on goal, blocked shots and misses) that a team takes while a player or team is on the ice.
explanation.incorrect: Corsi counts all shot attempts: shots on goal, blocked shots and misses. It's a stand-in for who controls play, not a count of goals or wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're over 55 percent Corsi, so they control most of the play.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of Corsi.
payload.template: Corsi counts all {{what}}, so a team above 50 percent usually {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Yes. Corsi counts every shot attempt, so a team over 50 percent is generating more of them and usually has more of the play.
explanation.incorrect: Corsi counts shot attempts, not goals. Being above 50 percent suggests more of the play, but it doesn't guarantee a win.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Their Corsi is 52 but they're losing 2-1. How is that possible?

payload.question: What might be going on?

options.text: They're getting plenty of attempts, but the shots may be weak or the goalie is hot.
options.explanation: Correct. Corsi counts volume, not quality, so a team can out-attempt the other side and still trail.

options.text: Corsi means nothing, only goals count.
options.explanation: Corsi is useful, but it's volume, not quality. It just can't explain every game.

options.text: A team over 50 percent Corsi can't be losing.
options.explanation: It can. Corsi doesn't include shot quality, goaltending or luck.

payload.translation: A team can have more of the play and still be behind when its shots are low quality or the other goalie is playing well.

followUps.line: Are their shots mostly from the perimeter?
followUps.why: It gets at shot quality versus shot volume.
A hot goalie can cancel out a lot of shot volume.

payload.prompt: A team with 48 percent Corsi can still win the game. True or false?

scene.alt: A team with fewer shot attempts but a higher-scoring game.

explanation.correct: True. Corsi counts shot attempts, not quality. A team can be out-attempted and still win with better chances or a hot goalie.
explanation.incorrect: Corsi is volume, not the quality of chances. A team that is out-attempted can still win by scoring on better chances or getting great goaltending.
explanation.sayThisLine: They were out-attempted, but they won the battle in the slot.

payload.prompt: Match the possession stat to its definition.

pairs.definition: Share of shot attempts (shots, blocks, misses) a team takes while a player or team is on the ice.
Like Corsi but excludes blocked shots; a 'cleaner' look at possession.
Stats that estimate who controls play, using shot attempts: volume, not quality.

explanation.summary: Corsi and Fenwick are possession stats. They show who had more of the play, not who won the game, and neither measures shot quality.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're well over 50 percent at five-on-five, so they're controlling the game.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We had 40 shots and only scored 1. The goalie robbed us.

payload.question: How would you explain the gap?

options.text: Check the xG. If it's around 2.5, the goalie or bad luck kept it at one.
options.explanation: Correct. Expected goals tells you how good the shots were, so you can tell whether the goalie or luck made the difference.

options.text: Shots are all that matter, so it must be a fluke.
options.explanation: Forty shots sounds like a lot, but many could be low quality. xG separates volume from quality.

options.text: Forty shots always means at least three goals.
options.explanation: It doesn't. Shots vary in quality, and goalies vary too.

payload.translation: Expected goals measures the quality of the shots. If xG is well above the goals scored, the other goalie played well or the team had bad luck.

followUps.line: What was the expected goals total?
followUps.why: It shows whether volume or quality was the issue.

followUps.line: How many of those were from the slot?
followUps.why: High-danger chances say a lot about how good the goalie was.

payload.prompt: What is PDO?

options.text: A penalty for diving or embellishment.
Shooting percentage plus save percentage; it tends toward 100.
A player's plus-minus divided by games played.

explanation.correct: Exactly. PDO adds a team's shooting percentage and its save percentage. Across a league it averages about 100, so a number far from 100 often points to luck.
explanation.incorrect: PDO combines how often a team scores on its shots and how often its goalie saves the shots against. The league average is about 100, and big departures from it usually fade.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their PDO is way up at 103, so some of that is luck.

payload.prompt: What is a typical PDO for a league-average team over a season?

explanation.correct: Right. The league average is about 100 by definition, and most teams end up close to it. A team sitting at 103 early usually drifts back as the luck evens out.
explanation.incorrect: PDO centers on 100. Extremes, high or low, tend to move back toward it over a season.
explanation.sayThisLine: That PDO is bound to come back toward 100.

payload.prompt: If a team's xG is 3.2 but they scored 4 goals, they performed better than their shot quality predicts. True or false?

scene.alt: A team scoring more goals than expected goals suggests outperforming the model.

explanation.correct: True. Scoring 4 on 3.2 expected goals means they scored more than their shots were worth, thanks to good finishing, good luck or a weak goalie.
explanation.incorrect: They scored more goals than the shot-quality model expected, so they beat the model on the night, by skill, luck or both.
explanation.sayThisLine: They scored four on three expected goals, so that finish was a bit lucky.

payload.prompt: Complete the PDO definition.
payload.template: PDO adds a team's {{a}} percentage to its {{b}} percentage, and a number far from 100 often signals {{c}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. PDO is shooting percentage plus save percentage. When it's far from 100, luck is often part of the story and it tends to even out.
explanation.incorrect: PDO is a team's shooting percentage plus its save percentage. Numbers far from 100 usually include some luck, which tends to regress.

lessons.title: Special teams percentages and faceoffs
lessons.objective: Read PP%, PK% and faceoff percentage.

payload.prompt: What does a power play percentage of 22 percent mean?

options.text: The team scores on 22 out of every 100 power plays.
22 percent of the team's goals come on power plays.
The other team has a 22 percent chance of scoring.

explanation.correct: Right. PP% is power-play goals divided by power-play opportunities. The league average is around 20 percent, so 22 is a little above average and 25 or more is elite.
explanation.incorrect: Power play percentage is a simple ratio: goals on the power play divided by power plays taken. It isn't the share of all goals or a chance for the other team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their power play is over 25 percent, so it's a real weapon.

payload.prompt: What is an average penalty kill percentage in the NHL?

explanation.correct: Around 80 percent. That means the average team stops about four out of five power plays.
explanation.incorrect: The league-average penalty kill is about 80 percent. Much above that is strong; well below it is a problem.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their penalty kill is in the low 80s, which is solid.

payload.prompt: Match the stat to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Goals on the power play divided by power play opportunities; 20% is average, 25%+ is elite.
Penalties survived without a goal divided by total penalties; 80% is average.
The share of faceoffs a player or team wins; it helps with puck possession, especially on special teams.

explanation.summary: Power play and penalty kill percentages show how a team does in special-teams moments, which often swing close games. Faceoff percentage is the same idea for draws.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their special teams are 25 percent on the power play and 82 on the kill.

payload.prompt: A center who wins 58 percent of faceoffs is below average. True or false?

scene.alt: A center taking faceoffs in the defensive zone.

explanation.correct: False. Fifty percent is average, so a center at 58 percent is very good. The best faceoff men are near 60.
explanation.incorrect: 58 percent is well above average, because 50 percent is the midpoint. Centers who win around 55 to 60 percent are the best on draws.
explanation.sayThisLine: He wins nearly 60 percent of his draws, which is elite.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Their power play is clicking at 26 percent, and the kill is at 79.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: The power play is excellent, and the penalty kill is about average.
options.explanation: Correct. 26 percent on the power play is elite, and 79 percent on the kill is right around league average.

options.text: Both special teams are struggling.
options.explanation: No. 26 percent on the power play is well above the league average of about 20.

options.text: The power play is average, and the penalty kill is elite.
options.explanation: That's flipped. The power play is the strong unit here, and the kill is around average.

payload.translation: Their power play scores on about a quarter of its chances, which is excellent, and their penalty kill stops about four out of five, which is about average.

followUps.line: Who runs the point on that power play?
followUps.why: It's a natural follow-up about the player who quarterbacks the unit.

followUps.line: Has the penalty kill been good lately?
followUps.why: It's a fair question about the weaker of the two units.

lessons.title: The salary cap
lessons.objective: Explain the cap and cap hit.

payload.prompt: What is the salary cap?

options.text: A league-set ceiling on how much a team can spend on its players in total.
The highest salary any single player can earn.
A suggestion teams follow to stay competitive.

explanation.correct: Yes. The NHL has a hard cap: a team's payroll has to stay under a league-set ceiling, apart from narrow exceptions like LTIR. The ceiling changes each year.
explanation.incorrect: The cap is a team-wide ceiling, not a cap on one player and not a suggestion. That's why trades and signings are cap decisions.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a cap problem, so they'll have to move salary out.

payload.prompt: A player signs a 7-year contract worth $56 million total. What is his cap hit?

options.text: $56 million.
$8 million per year (the average annual value).
$4 million per year.

explanation.correct: Right. Cap hit is the contract's average annual value. $56 million over seven years is $8 million a year against the cap.
explanation.incorrect: Cap hit is the average annual value: total contract value divided by years. $56 million over seven years is $8 million.
explanation.sayThisLine: His cap hit is $8 million, even if his actual pay varies year to year.

payload.prompt: Estimate the 2026-27 NHL salary cap ceiling.

explanation.correct: Nice. The ceiling for 2026-27 is $104 million. It moves from year to year with league revenue and the labor agreement, so the number is worth re-checking each summer.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026-27 ceiling is $104 million. It changes from year to year with league revenue and the labor agreement.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cap is around a hundred million, so a big contract is a big deal.

payload.prompt: Complete the statement about cap hits.
payload.template: A cap hit is a contract's {{what}} counted against the cap, so a big one {{impact}} a team's flexibility.

explanation.correct: Yes. A cap hit is the average annual value, and a big one takes up room a team could use to add or keep other players.
explanation.incorrect: Cap hit is average annual value, not just salary or bonus. A large one limits what else a team can fit under the cap.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: They want to sign a star but they're $2M over the cap.

payload.question: What can they do?

options.text: Move salary out, by trade or other roster moves, to make room.
options.explanation: Correct. Under a hard cap, a team has to clear room before it can add salary.

options.text: Sign him anyway and pay a fine.
options.explanation: It doesn't work like that. The cap is a hard ceiling, not a soft penalty.

options.text: Exceed the cap for the whole season.
options.explanation: A team can't stay over the cap. Only narrow exceptions, like LTIR, give room.

payload.translation: The cap is a hard ceiling. To add salary, a team has to shed payroll first.

followUps.line: Who would they trade to make room?
followUps.why: It's a natural question: usually someone with a sizable cap hit.
It shows you know there's a narrow exception for long-term injuries.

payload.prompt: Match the roster tool to its use.

pairs.definition: A cap exception that lets a team replace an injured player's cap hit while he is out long term.
A process where other teams can claim a player before he is sent to the minors or released.
A healthy player left out of the lineup that night; his salary still counts against the cap.

explanation.summary: LTIR, waivers and healthy scratches are everyday roster tools. LTIR is also a hot topic, because fans argue about how teams use the cap room it creates.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're using LTIR to make room for a star.

payload.prompt: What allows a team to use LTIR?

options.text: A player is injured and expected to miss a long stretch, at least 10 games and 24 days.
The league commissioner approves it for any reason.
A team votes to use it.

explanation.correct: Right. LTIR needs a documented injury that keeps a player out for at least 10 games and 24 days. It isn't a vote or a favor.
explanation.incorrect: LTIR requires a real, documented long-term injury. A commissioner's whim or a team vote doesn't qualify a player.
explanation.sayThisLine: When he's healthy again, they'll have to fit him under the cap.

payload.prompt: When another team claims a player off waivers, his old team gets players or picks back. True or false?

scene.alt: A player going through the waiver process before being sent down.

explanation.correct: False. A claim isn't a trade. The team that claims the player simply takes him and his contract, and the old team gets nothing back.
explanation.incorrect: A waiver claim is not a trade, so no players or picks change hands. The claiming team takes him and his contract as he is.
explanation.sayThisLine: He went on waivers and got claimed, so they got nothing for him.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: They're over the cap. Their backup D-man just went on LTIR so they can add a star.

payload.question: What is going on?

options.text: LTIR frees up cap room while the injured player is out.
options.explanation: Correct. While he's on LTIR, his cap hit can be replaced, which gives the team room to add a player.

options.text: They broke the cap rule and will be punished.
options.explanation: No. LTIR is an allowed exception for players who are hurt long term.

options.text: The defenseman was traded away.
options.explanation: LTIR is an injury status, not a trade.

payload.translation: An injured player on long-term injured reserve opens cap room for a team, so they can add a player even though they were at the cap. Fans often argue about how teams use this.

followUps.line: Is he really out long term?
followUps.why: LTIR needs a documented injury, so the question matters.
It moves the chat to the exciting part, the new player.

payload.prompt: If a player clears waivers (no team claims him), what happens next?

options.text: He can be sent to the AHL minor league or released.
He must stay in the NHL but is a free agent.
He is traded immediately.

explanation.correct: Yes. Once he clears, the team can assign him to its AHL affiliate or waive or release him. Waivers exist so other teams get a shot at him first.
explanation.incorrect: Clearing waivers means no team claimed him, so his team can send him to the minors or release him. He doesn't become a free agent automatically.
explanation.sayThisLine: He cleared waivers, so he's headed to the AHL.

payload.prompt: What does the NHL draft select?

options.text: Young prospects, mostly 18-year-olds from junior, college and European leagues.
Free agents who have played professional hockey for 10+ years.
International players only.

explanation.correct: Right. The draft is where teams pick young prospects, mostly 18-year-olds from junior leagues, US development programs and European clubs.
explanation.incorrect: The draft is for young, unsigned prospects, most of them 18, not veterans or free agents. Teams then develop them before they play in the NHL.
explanation.sayThisLine: They took him in the first round at eighteen.

payload.prompt: Order the typical path for a drafted player to reach the NHL.

items.text: The player is drafted by an NHL team at age 18.
items.why: Draft selections happen in June; the player enters the prospect pipeline.

items.text: He keeps developing in junior, college or a European league for a few years.
items.why: Most drafted players need time before they're ready for pro hockey.

items.text: He often plays for the team's AHL affiliate, the minor league.
items.why: The AHL is a common step between junior hockey and the NHL, though top prospects can skip it.

items.text: He is called up to the NHL and plays his first games.
items.why: The NHL debut is the end of the pipeline.

explanation.correct: That's the usual path: draft, develop, a stop in the AHL, then the NHL. Some stars skip steps, and many prospects never make it.
explanation.incorrect: The usual order is draft, development in junior, college or Europe, the AHL, and then the NHL. Star prospects can skip a step.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's still in the pipeline, so he's a year or two away.

payload.prompt: How many rounds does the NHL draft have?

explanation.correct: Seven. Each team holds one pick per round unless it has traded some, so top picks in round one matter most and later rounds are long shots.
explanation.incorrect: The draft runs seven rounds. Each team starts with one pick per round, and teams trade picks, so the totals vary.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a first-round pick, so he's a real prospect.

payload.prompt: The lottery is a system where the worst team is guaranteed to pick first in the draft. True or false?

scene.alt: Lottery balls being drawn to determine draft order.

explanation.correct: False. The lottery is random. The worst teams have the best odds, but a team that didn't finish last can win the top pick.
explanation.incorrect: The worst team isn't guaranteed the first pick. The lottery gives the worst teams the best odds, which is meant to discourage tanking.
explanation.sayThisLine: They finished last but the lottery didn't give them the first pick.

payload.prompt: Match the draft concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The annual event where teams select young prospects, in an order set partly by a lottery.
A random draw for the top picks; the worst teams get the best odds, which discourages tanking.
A team's stream of drafted players developing in junior, college, Europe and the AHL.

explanation.summary: The draft restocks a team with young players, the lottery shapes the top of the order, and the pipeline is how those players develop over years.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their prospect pipeline is deep, so the future looks good.

payload.prompt: Match the on-screen stat abbreviation to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Corsi percentage: the share of shot attempts while a player or team is on the ice.
Time on ice; the minutes a player played in the game.
Faceoff percentage; the share of draws won by a player or team.

explanation.summary: Broadcast graphics pack a lot into a few letters. TOI is usage, CF% is who has the shot attempts, and FO% is how a player fares on draws.
explanation.sayThisLine: His CF% is strong, so they've had the shot attempts when he's out there.

payload.prompt: Complete the interpretation of broadcast stats.
payload.template: A center with {{toi}} of TOI, {{cf}} CF% and {{fo}} FO% looks like a trusted top-line player.

explanation.correct: Right. About 20 minutes means he's trusted, a Corsi above 50 means his team has the puck, and winning most draws helps too.
explanation.incorrect: A trusted top-line center plays heavy minutes, sits above 50 in Corsi and wins more than half his faceoffs.

statement.speaker: You
statement.text: On the broadcast graphic, you see a forward with 14 minutes TOI and 42% Corsi.

payload.question: What does that tell you about his night?

options.text: His team was out-attempted while he was on the ice, and 14 minutes is a normal role for a depth forward.
options.explanation: Correct. A 42 percent Corsi means his team had fewer shot attempts when he played, and 14 minutes is typical for a third- or fourth-liner.

options.text: He played over 20 minutes as a star.
options.explanation: Fourteen minutes isn't star usage for a forward. Top forwards play closer to 18 or more.

options.text: He won 42 percent of his faceoffs.
options.explanation: That mixes up two stats. Corsi is shot attempts; faceoff percentage is labeled FO%.

payload.translation: His team took fewer shot attempts than the other side with him on the ice. That's one night and one stat, and 14 minutes is a normal depth role.

followUps.line: Who was he lined up against?
followUps.why: It shows you know matchups affect Corsi.
Corsi is noisy in one game, so a player's usual numbers matter more.

payload.prompt: A center's FO% is 39 percent on the broadcast graphic. What does that mean?

options.text: He won 39 out of 100 faceoffs; he is below average on draws.
He lost 39 percent of his shifts.
He touched the puck 39 percent of the time.

explanation.correct: Right. FO% is the share of faceoffs a player wins. 50 percent is average, so a center at 39 percent is losing a lot of draws.
explanation.incorrect: FO% is the percentage of draws won, nothing to do with shifts or touches. Around 50 is average, and 39 is well below it.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's struggling on faceoffs tonight, at 39 percent.

payload.prompt: A defenseman with 25 minutes and 51% Corsi held even on shot attempts in heavy minutes. True or false?

scene.alt: Broadcast showing stats for a defenseman who is close to even in possession.

explanation.correct: True. Fifty percent is even, so 51 percent on 25 minutes means his team held its own while he played a lot, often against tough opposition.
explanation.incorrect: Fifty percent Corsi is break-even, so 51 is a touch better than even. On 25 minutes that's a solid night, not a bad one.
explanation.sayThisLine: He held even in 25 minutes, which is a solid night for a defenseman.

payload.prompt: Match the contract term to its definition.

pairs.definition: A player on an expiring contract, acquired before the deadline to help a team's playoff run.
A clause that limits where a team can trade a player; a full one lets him veto any trade.
A veteran whose contract has expired and who can sign with any team once free agency opens.

explanation.summary: Contract terms decide how easily a player can move. A rental is temporary, a no-trade clause limits trades and a UFA can pick his team.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's a rental, so he could be gone in the summer.

payload.prompt: When does free agency begin in the NHL?

options.text: July 1 at noon.
The day after the Stanley Cup is awarded.
January 1.

explanation.correct: Right. Free agency opens on July 1 at noon Eastern, and a lot of the big signings happen within hours.
explanation.incorrect: Free agency opens on July 1 at noon Eastern. That's when unrestricted free agents can sign with any team, not after the Cup or on New Year's Day.
explanation.sayThisLine: Free agency opens July 1, so that's when the big signings land.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: A star signed a long deal with a full no-trade clause.

payload.question: What is the advantage to him?

options.text: The team can't trade him without his approval.
options.explanation: Correct. A full no-trade clause means any trade needs his yes.

options.text: It pays him extra money each year.
options.explanation: The clause is about control, not pay, although players sometimes trade salary for it.

options.text: He can leave whenever he wants.
options.explanation: It limits trades by the team. It doesn't let him walk away from the contract.

payload.translation: A no-trade clause protects the player. The team can't trade him without his approval, so he picks whether and where he moves.

followUps.line: Is it a full no-trade or a limited one?
followUps.why: It shows you know some clauses only cover a list of teams.

followUps.line: Would he waive it for a contender?
followUps.why: Players can waive a clause for a particular trade, which is how many deals happen.

payload.prompt: Can the team trade a star with a limited no-trade clause?

situation.narrative: Your team wants to trade a star who has a limited no-trade clause. A contender has offered a good package, but it isn't on the list of teams he has approved.

facts.label: Contract
facts.value: Long-term deal with a limited no-trade clause

facts.label: Offer
facts.value: A contender not on his approved list

facts.label: Star's view
facts.value: Would consider it if the team is a contender

options.label: Ask him to waive the clause for that team
options.consequence: If he agrees, the trade can go through. If he says no, the trade is off, so the team has to sell him on it.
considerations: A player can waive his clause for one trade.
The clause gives him the final say on that destination.

options.label: Trade him anyway, since the team owns the contract
options.consequence: The trade isn't valid without his consent. The clause is part of the contract.
considerations: The team agreed to the clause when it signed him.
A trade like that would be rejected.

options.label: Treat the contract as void and let him walk
options.consequence: A no-trade clause doesn't void a contract. It only limits trades.

payload.expertNote: A no-trade clause gives a player real leverage, because the team can only trade him where he agrees. That's why you'll hear about players 'waiving' a clause to join a contender.

payload.prompt: An RFA's team can match any offer sheet from another team. True or false?

scene.alt: A team exercising its right to match an offer sheet in order to retain the player.

explanation.correct: True. A restricted free agent's team can match an offer sheet, which keeps the player. If it doesn't match, the other team gets him but owes draft picks back.
explanation.incorrect: An RFA's current team has the right to match an offer sheet from another team and keep the player. If it lets him go, it gets draft-pick compensation.
explanation.sayThisLine: They'll match the offer sheet, so he's staying.
